messages.subject: Time now() in a trajectory.
parts:
Hi Shawn,

Of course it is, whenever you define the environment *before* running the simulation. For instance, this won't work:

t <- create_trajectory() %>%
  timeout(function() print(env %>% now()))

env <- simmer() %>%
  add_generator("dummy", t, function() 1) %>%
  run(4)
Because the global "env" is not available at runtime: the simulation runs *and then* the resulting object is assigned to "env". You need to assign first, then run. So this will work:
t <- create_trajectory() %>%
  timeout(function() print(env %>% now()))

env <- simmer() %>%
  add_generator("dummy", t, function() 1)

env %>% run(4)
And you'll get "1, 2, 3", as expected. However, as a general rule of good practice, I recommend you to instantiate the environment always in the first place, because the code becomes more readable:
# First, instantiate the environment
env <- simmer()

# Here I'm using it
t <- create_trajectory() %>%
  timeout(function() print(env %>% now()))

# And finally, run it
env %>%
  add_generator("dummy", t, function() 1) %>%
  run(3)

Regards,
Iñaki


2016-04-27 16:20 GMT+02:00 Garbett, Shawn P <>:
Iñaki Úcar,

Is it possible to check the current time of a simulation inside a trajectory? The now() function depends on an environment, not the current trajectory.

Shawn Garbett | Sr. App Developer | Biostatistics | Vanderbilt University

parts:
And for the sake of completeness, here it is another set of examples, very related to this issue, in response to Lindsay Mico:

First, I'd like to use functions in the simulation based on the current sim time.  The most obvious use would to be create a generator function that is dependent on what the current time is in the simulation.  In my experiments with now(), I have been successful using it after the simulation has been run, but not embedding it into either the trajectory or the generator. 
env <- simmer("SuperDuperSim") # you may do this at the beginning as a general rule of good practice
 
t0 <- create_trajectory("my trajectory") %>%
  timeout(0)
 
my_generator <- function() {
  if (now(env) %% 5 == 0)
    print(sprintf("now() is a multiple of 5: %f", now(env)))
  1 # one time unit between arrivals
}
 
env %>%
  add_generator("instant-traveler", t0, my_generator) %>%
  run(until=10)
A related question is how to run user defined functions inside a simulation.  For example, it would be useful to export a plot every time an entity reaches a given point in a trajectory.

This one is funny. :)
library(animation)
 
env <- simmer("SuperDuperSim")
 
plot_and_wait <- function() {
  if (now(env) > 1)
    print(plot_resource_usage(env, "checkin", steps=T))
  rnorm(1, mean = 7, sd = 2)
}
 
t0 <- create_trajectory("my trajectory") %>%
  seize("checkin", 1) %>%
  timeout(plot_and_wait) %>%
  release("checkin", 1)
 
env %>%
  add_generator("traveler", t0, function() rexp(1,rate=.625)) %>%
  add_resource("checkin", 5)
 
# use your own path here for the GIF
saveGIF(run(env, until=50), interval = .2, movie.name="trace.gif")
 
Or even to change the structure of the trajectory itself based on queue size or wait time.

You cannot change the trajectory object, but you can define many options in one with a branch:
env <- simmer("SuperDuperSim")
 
decide <- function() {
  if (env %>% get_queue_count("checkin") <= 3)
    1         # first trajectory of the branch
  else 2   # second trajectory of the branch
}
 
t0 <- create_trajectory("my trajectory") %>%
  branch(decide, merge=c(T, T),
         create_trajectory("seize") %>%
           seize("checkin", 1) %>%
           timeout(1) %>%
           release("checkin", 1),
         create_trajectory("skip") %>%
           timeout(function() { print("So much travellers waiting... I desist"); 0 })
         )
 
env %>%
  add_generator("traveler", t0, function() rexp(1,rate=.625)) %>%
  add_resource("checkin", 1) %>%
  run()
 
Last question - as an experiment I tried writing a for loop that calls onestep n times, increments a counter variable 'test'.  In the code below I had hoped to assign this variable as an attribute at each step.  However as far as I can tell, the actual value of the variable is assigned at the time the environment is instantiated, rather than simply the variable itself.  If this doesn't make sense let me know.  

As in all previous examples, you need to define a function for the set_attribute activity, not a static value:

env <- simmer("SuperDuperSim")
 
t0 <- create_trajectory("my trajectory") %>%
  timeout(function() runif(1, min=2, max=3)) %>%
  seize("checkin", 1) %>%
  set_attribute("test", function() test) %>%
  timeout(function() rnorm(1, mean = 7, sd = 2)) %>%
  release("checkin", 1)
 
env %>%
  add_resource("checkin", 5) %>%
  add_generator("traveler", t0, function() rexp(1,rate=.625),mon = 2)
 
test <- 0
for(i in 1:100){
 
  env<-onestep(env)
  test <- test+1
  print(test)
}
 
get_mon_attributes(env)

Regards,
Iñaki

parts:
This is proving to be a problem for me. 'env' as a global variable is now forcing my model inputs to be a global as well.

I have a list of "inputs". These control trajectory behavior through permutations to compare. So, I wrote a function where the patient trajectory is a function of inputs. Now, if I reset the global env, the generator's that were added are still present. The only solution is to now make inputs a global variable as well, since I can't way to delete a previously defined generator.

So, now 'env' and 'inputs' are now forced to be global objects. I prefer a more functional approach that doesn't depend on environment globals.

The best solution to all this is if there was a 'now()' function that worked in a trajectory and it didn't depend on accessing a global variable.

I don't have a fully working example, but here goes my best attempt at showing what I'm working on:

library(simmer)

env <- simmer("Global Env for now() to work") # Not used in this example, but main code needs this

# Configuration for model run, will be called from another R package with this info
# Doing this as a global
input <- TRUE

# Create some resources
env %>% add_resource("life", Inf, 0)

# May terminate
event <- function(traj)
{
  traj %>% branch(
    function() sample(1:2, 1, prob=c(0.8,0.2)),
    merge=c(TRUE,FALSE),
    create_trajectory() %>% timeout(1), # Something non-fatal happened
    create_trajectory() %>% release("life")
  )
}

traj <- create_trajectory() %>%
        seize("life") %>%
        branch(function() input+1,
               merge=c(FALSE,TRUE),
               create_trajectory() %>%
                 timeout(40) %>%
                 release("life"),
               create_trajectory() %>%
                 event()
        ) %>%
        rollback(amount=1, times=100) 

env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)

run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf
  env %>% reset() %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE)

run_sim(FALSE) # NO OUTPUT!!!!, doesn't matter if configuration is flipped, the 2nd run is empty

# Well that didn't work, now for hacked permutative guessing
run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf

  env %>% reset()
  env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)
  env %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE) # Still no output, probably didn't need to add generator

# Hack #2, Seems to work--but does weird things in a larger simulation around resources.
run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf

  # Blow global environment away!!!  
  env <- simmer("Global Env for now() to work") # And it complains that it already is defined
  env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)
  env %>% add_resource("life", Inf, 0)
  env %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE)

run_sim(FALSE)

Hack #2 appears to work in this example, but at the expense of blowing away the environment. However, in my larger code base, the first model run works great. Then in the Hack #2 run, it doesn't always release resources, even when run with the same input!

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Re: Time now() in a trajectory.
parts: Ok, thanks, I see. Several things here:

env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)

run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf
  env %>% reset() %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}

• That wrap() above is useless there, because 1) you are not assigning the result to any variable (wrapped <- env %>% ... %>% wrap()) and 2) you don’t really need it in this case.
  • The line input <- conf is NOT changing the global variable input. You are creating a local one with the same name, and the trajectory, as it is defined in a parent scope, uses the parent input, not that one. If you want to change the global input, you need to do input <<- conf. Note the double arrow assignment operator.
  • The reset() function is not resetting the generator function, so at(...) generates its 10 arrivals in the first run and that’s it. This is a bug and that’s why you are not getting results in the second run. Thank you, I’ll open an issue and I’ll fix it in the next release. ;-)

In the meantime, the hack #2 should work well. In fact, it’s not a hack at all. I mean, it’s just fine to define a new environment for each new simulation. It’s a hard reset. But in order to be able to use now() inside a trajectory defined in a parent scope, again, you need to use the double arrow assignment:

run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <<- conf # Change global conf
# Redefine the parent environment. This should not complain about anything
env <<- simmer("Global Env for now() to work"

) 
  env %>% 
    add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2) %>%
    add_resource("life", Inf, 0) %>%
    run(36500) %>% # useless wrap() removed
    get_mon_arrivals(per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE)

run_sim(FALSE)

If you don’t want global variables at all, then you can define the trajectory inside run_sim() and switch back to single arrow assignments.

​

parts:
As far as I know, <- never assigns to globals in any circumstances. From the help (? assignOps):

The operators <- and = assign into the environment in which they are evaluated. The operator <- can be used anywhere, whereas the operator = is only allowed at the top level (e.g., in the complete expression typed at the command prompt) or as one of the subexpressions in a braced list of expressions.

The operators <<- and ->> are normally only used in functions, and cause a search to be made through parent environments for an existing definition of the variable being assigned. If such a variable is found (and its binding is not locked) then its value is redefined, otherwise assignment takes place in the global environment.

​
2016-05-20 16:38 GMT+02:00 Shawn Garbett <shawn....@gmail.com>:

Wow, works like a charm. The <<- and <- I understand, but the <- assigns to globals in some circumstances. However, it's far better to be explicit.

On Fri, May 20, 2016 at 7:48 AM, Iñaki Úcar <i.uc...@gmail.com> wrote:

Ok, thanks, I see. Several things here:

env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)

run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf
  env %>% reset() %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}
  • That wrap() above is useless there, because 1) you are not assigning the result to any variable (wrapped <- env %>% ... %>% wrap()) and 2) you don’t really need it in this case.
  • The line input <- conf is NOT changing the global variable input. You are creating a local one with the same name, and the trajectory, as it is defined in a parent scope, uses the parent input, not that one. If you want to change the global input, you need to do input <<- conf. Note the double arrow assignment operator.
  • The reset() function is not resetting the generator function, so at(...) generates its 10 arrivals in the first run and that’s it. This is a bug and that’s why you are not getting results in the second run. Thank you, I’ll open an issue and I’ll fix it in the next release. ;-)

In the meantime, the hack #2 should work well. In fact, it’s not a hack at all. I mean, it’s just fine to define a new environment for each new simulation. It’s a hard reset. But in order to be able to use now() inside a trajectory defined in a parent scope, again, you need to use the double arrow assignment:

run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <<- conf # Change global conf

  # Redefine the parent environment. This should not complain about anything
  env <<- simmer("Global Env for now() to work") 
  env %>% 
    add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2) %>%
    add_resource("life", Inf, 0) %>%
    run(36500) %>% # useless wrap() removed
    get_mon_arrivals(per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE)

run_sim(FALSE)

If you don’t want global variables at all, then you can define the trajectory inside run_sim() and switch back to single arrow assignments.

​

I don't have a fully working example, but here goes my best attempt at showing what I'm working on:

library(simmer)

env <- simmer("Global Env for now() to work") # Not used in this example, but main code needs this

# Configuration for model run, will be called from another R package with this info
# Doing this as a global
input <- TRUE

# Create some resources
env %>% add_resource("life", Inf, 0)

# May terminate
event <- function(traj)
{
  traj %>% branch(
    function() sample(1:2, 1, prob=c(0.8,0.2)),
    merge=c(TRUE,FALSE),
    create_trajectory() %>% timeout(1), # Something non-fatal happened
    create_trajectory() %>% release("life")
  )
}

traj <- create_trajectory() %>%
        seize("life") %>%
        branch(function() input+1,
               merge=c(FALSE,TRUE),
               create_trajectory() %>%
                 timeout(40) %>%
                 release("life"),
               create_trajectory() %>%
                 event()
        ) %>%
        rollback(amount=1, times=100) 

env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)

run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf
  env %>% reset() %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE)

run_sim(FALSE) # NO OUTPUT!!!!, doesn't matter if configuration is flipped, the 2nd run is empty

# Well that didn't work, now for hacked permutative guessing
run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf

  env %>% reset()
  env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)
  env %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE) # Still no output, probably didn't need to add generator

# Hack #2, Seems to work--but does weird things in a larger simulation around resources.
run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf

  # Blow global environment away!!!  
  env <- simmer("Global Env for now() to work") # And it complains that it already is defined
  env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)
  env %>% add_resource("life", Inf, 0)
  env %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE)

run_sim(FALSE)

Hack #2 appears to work in this example, but at the expense of blowing away the environment. However, in my larger code base, the first model run works great. Then in the Hack #2 run, it doesn't always release resources, even when run with the same input!

This is proving to be a problem for me. 'env' as a global variable is now forcing my model inputs to be a global as well.

I have a list of "inputs". These control trajectory behavior through permutations to compare. So, I wrote a function where the patient trajectory is a function of inputs. Now, if I reset the global env, the generator's that were added are still present. The only solution is to now make inputs a global variable as well, since I can't way to delete a previously defined generator.

So, now 'env' and 'inputs' are now forced to be global objects. I prefer a more functional approach that doesn't depend on environment globals.

The best solution to all this is if there was a 'now()' function that worked in a trajectory and it didn't depend on accessing a global variable.
